content: Pyruvic acid, also known as CH3COCO2H, is classified as an alpha-keto acid. Its carboxylate anion form is referred to as pyruvate, which plays a critical role in various biochemical processes. Chemically, pyruvic acid is a colorless liquid with an odor resembling that of acetic acid. It is miscible with water and soluble in ethanol and diethyl ether. In laboratory settings, pyruvic acid can be synthesized by heating a mixture of tartaric acid and potassium hydrogen sulfate or through the hydrolysis of acetyl cyanide, which is produced by reacting acetyl chloride with potassium cyanide. Biochemically, pyruvate is a pivotal compound. It is the end product of glycolysis, the aerobic metabolism of glucose. During glycolysis, one molecule of glucose is broken down into two molecules of pyruvic acid. These pyruvate molecules can then be utilized to generate energy through two primary pathways. Pyruvic acid can be converted into acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA), which serves as the primary substrate for the Krebs cycle, a series of reactions essential for cellular respiration. Alternatively, pyruvate can be converted into oxaloacetate via an anaplerotic reaction, replenishing intermediates of the Krebs cycle or serving as a precursor for gluconeogenesis. The Krebs cycle, also known as the citric acid cycle, is named after Hans Adolf Krebs, who was awarded the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on metabolic processes. Under conditions of limited oxygen availability, pyruvic acid undergoes anaerobic breakdown. In animals, this process results in the formation of lactic acid, while in plants, it leads to the production of ethanol. During lactate fermentation, pyruvate is converted to lactate by the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase, with NADH serving as a coenzyme. In alcoholic fermentation, pyruvate is first converted to acetaldehyde and subsequently to ethanol. Pyruvic acid serves as a central hub in metabolic pathways, as it can be transformed into carbohydrates via gluconeogenesis, fatty acids or energy through acetyl-CoA, the amino acid alanine, or ethanol. This versatility allows pyruvic acid to integrate multiple key metabolic processes. A derivative of pyruvic acid, bromopyruvic acid, is currently being investigated for its potential applications in cancer treatment. Research led by Young Hee Ko at Johns Hopkins University and others explores its role in supporting the Warburg hypothesis, which posits that altered energy metabolism is a fundamental cause of cancer. In glycolysis, the enzyme pyruvate kinase catalyzes the conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to pyruvate. This reaction is highly exergonic and irreversible. In gluconeogenesis, the reverse transformation of pyruvate to PEP requires two enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase. It is important to note that the depiction of a reverse reaction arrow in some diagrams is incorrect. Pyruvate can also undergo decarboxylation to form acetyl-CoA, a reaction catalyzed by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. However, decarboxylation is just one of several possible reactions involving pyruvate. From an evolutionary perspective, current theories on the origin of life suggest that the first organisms were anaerobic, as the prebiotic Earth's atmosphere lacked significant oxygen. Consequently, essential biochemical materials must have existed prior to the emergence of life. Recent experiments demonstrate that pyruvate can be synthesized abiotically. In vitro, iron sulfide under sufficient pressure and temperature catalyzes the formation of pyruvic acid. Günter Wächtershäuser has proposed that the interaction of iron-rich crust with hydrothermal vent fluids may have provided the necessary conditions for the emergence of life.
